the US-led recognition of the independence of Kosovo in February, 2008, and the Russian-led recognitions of the independence of South Ossetian and Abkhazian in August, 2008 have not changed the norms of international society in any way, but they have introduced a great deal of confusion into them and have had important implications in other situations.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Kosovo and South Ossetia–Abkhazia cases have not altered the existing norms of international recognition but have, rather, complicated them and made them less clear.
the practice of recognition remains in a period of transition, but the transition has not led to the emergence of a new, clear-cut norm of recognition.
the contemporary practice of recognition has been changed by these three cases, but not in any way that would be expected from the perspective of the traditional practice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, although there has been no significant change in the existing practice of state recognition, the Kosovo and South Ossetia/Abkhazia episodes have introduced a new and highly problematic element into that practice.
the practice of state recognition has not changed, but it has been significantly complicated.
there is no evidence of any change in the existing rules and norms of recognition of statehood, but there is evidence that the practice is in flux.
The main takeaway from our work is that
recognition is not the simple, straightforward practice it once was.
, in a world of great power politics, recognition is still a powerful tool for the leading states, even in the absence of a clear normative framework.
, in the contemporary world of international relations, the practice of recognition is still a highly contested and uncertain process.
